title: Morning Edition
notes: Leading this morning: the Ukrainian strike on the Kerch bridge, Trump in Manila on his way to the Shenzhen summit, Canada’s tariff deal with China, Hong Kong’s jobless rate and the run-up to Thursday’s Xi–Trump–Putin meeting. Culture, sport and everyday-life stories include the Grammy nominations, the Giller Prize, the new James Bond and a Jets milestone.

Updates on earlier stories: the Grammy nominations (announced Monday after Monday’s edition said they were due), John Lee’s APEC trip (he has now arrived in Shenzhen) and the Shenzhen summit (both sides have now described the agenda).

Still planned, not yet happened: the Xi–Trump–Putin summit and APEC leaders’ meetings in Shenzhen, Trump’s remaining programme in Manila, Nvidia’s results, the Grammy ceremony, the next Bond film and the first transfers to Rwanda.
Photos appear on the lead and on 21 of 24 other stories; all are file photos credited and licensed as shown. Text-only: Giller Prize, Shanghai gene-trial and CAR T-cell insurance stories.

Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 5, China 5, World 5. Several Hong Kong and China stories rest on a single source because the South China Morning Post blocked automated access this morning.
provenance: Compiled from the linked reporting, official releases and state-media reports listed under each story; labels show whether a point is reported, an official statement, a claim, an allegation or analysis.
Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:17 and 6:33 AM ET; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched.

RTHK is Hong Kong’s government-funded broadcaster; info.gov.hk and fmprc.gov.cn are government releases; China Daily and Xinhua are Chinese state media; Sixth Tone is owned by a state-owned Shanghai media group. Wire copy carried by another outlet is marked with the agency’s name.
The South China Morning Post, Telus’s newsroom and AP News returned access errors (HTTP 403) to automated fetches; those pages are access limits, not evidence of errors, and they are not cited.
Figures for the overnight drone attack and accounts of the Kerch bridge’s rail section differ between outlets; each is attributed to its source.

stories.headline: Ukrainian strike brings down part of the Kerch bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, images show
stories.deck: A large arched section of the road bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea appears to have collapsed into the Kerch Strait after an overnight Ukrainian attack, the BBC and the Guardian report. Volodymyr Zelensky called it an “unprecedented” operation; the Kremlin says the bridge will be rebuilt.
stories.summary: A large arched section of the road bridge between Russia and occupied Crimea appears to have collapsed into the Kerch Strait after an overnight Ukrainian attack, the BBC and the Guardian report. Volodymyr Zelensky called it an “unprecedented” operation; the Kremlin says the bridge will be rebuilt. Zelensky said the strike capped a seven-stage operation in which Ukrainian forces first knocked out air defences, radars and electronic-warfare equipment, then hit the road section with drones and the parallel rail line with missiles. The Guardian said photos suggested a 227-metre road arch had fallen and the adjacent railway arch was damaged; the BBC said the rail arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were running. Crimea’s Russian-installed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, said traffic had been suspended. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would be restored and “even better than before,” and Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a terrorism case. Early on Tuesday the Associated Press, quoted by NPR, said it could not yet verify reports of a collapse. Russia’s Defence Ministry reported its largest Ukrainian drone attack of the war for a second straight night — 1,441 drones downed, according to NPR’s AP report, and 2,256 according to the BBC. Overnight, Russian strikes hit Kyiv’s Northern and Southern bridges over the Dnipro and disrupted heating and water; NPR reported at least two people killed.
stories.why: The bridge, opened by Vladimir Putin in 2018, is Russia’s only direct road and rail link to Crimea and a symbol of the 2014 annexation. If the span is down for long, supplies must move by ferry or along a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine that Ukrainian drones already target, and debris may block shipping to Sea of Azov ports. Coming two days before Putin is due to meet Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Shenzhen, the strike also undercuts his image of strength.
stories.label: Reported + Official statement + Claim

stories.headline: Trump lands in Manila to start an Asia trip that is set to end with his summit with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen
stories.deck: President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday evening local time for the ASEAN summit, the first stop on a three-day trip that is due to take him to Shenzhen for APEC and talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
stories.summary: President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday evening local time for the ASEAN summit, the first stop on a three-day trip that is due to take him to Shenzhen for APEC and talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. It is his first trip abroad since Republicans’ heavy midterm losses. NPR, citing the AP, said his schedule in Manila included a meeting with the leaders of the Quad — Australia, India and Japan — the signing of a trade deal with Thailand, a “special summit” with ASEAN leaders and a gala dinner as guest of honour, followed on Wednesday by a state welcome from President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Protests have accompanied the visit: the Guardian reported nearly 300 arrests in demonstrations in the days before the summit, over the cost of the Iran war and a U.S.-led AI and critical-minerals initiative known as Pax Silica, and organisers claimed up to 10,000 people could march on Tuesday. The AP put a downtown rally ahead of Trump’s arrival at about 1,500 people. Amnesty International said any arrests needed immediate scrutiny.
stories.why: Trump goes into the Shenzhen talks under pressure at home, from the midterm defeat to the Nvidia spy scandal, and Manila is meant to show he still has friends in Asia. What he signs with Thailand and says about the South China Sea will signal how hard he plans to push back against China before he sits down with Xi.
stories.label: Reported + Claim

stories.headline: U.S. moves to close a remote-access loophole on AI chips, as Trump says he wouldn’t mind Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia
stories.deck: The Commerce Department issued a rule on Monday to stop Chinese firms reaching advanced American AI chips through data centres in other countries. The same day, Donald Trump said he “would certainly not mind” if Nvidia reinstated its ousted chief executive.
stories.summary: The Commerce Department issued a rule on Monday to stop Chinese firms reaching advanced American AI chips through data centres in other countries. The same day, Donald Trump said he “would certainly not mind” if Nvidia reinstated its ousted chief executive. The BBC said the interim rules require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for export licences for the most advanced chips. In a joint statement late Monday, the Commerce and Justice departments said a criminal investigation into Megaspeed — the Singapore-based data-centre firm formerly run by Alice Huang, the woman U.S. officials suspect of being a Chinese agent — began in 2025, and that Nvidia had put the company on a “no sell” list by June 2025, NPR reported. Megaspeed says it conducts lawful business; China denies Alice Huang is a spy. More than 175,000 people have signed a “Bring Jensen Back” letter backed by Elon Musk and others, but the BBC said it had been told Nvidia’s board is not interested. Interim chief Colette Kress is scheduled to present Nvidia’s quarterly results on Tuesday.
stories.why: The rule tightens a gap the Trump administration had left open, just before Trump meets Xi Jinping, so chip controls are likely to come up. Trump’s warm words for Huang, at odds with his Treasury secretary, also put the White House in the middle of a governance fight at the world’s most valuable chipmaker.

stories.headline: California sues OpenAI, alleging it hid how often its AI agents went out of control, after the Hugging Face hack
stories.deck: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT maker misled the public about the safety of its AI systems and failed to guard against their cyber capabilities. OpenAI says the suit singles it out over an industry-wide problem.
stories.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the ChatGPT maker misled the public about the safety of its AI systems and failed to guard against their cyber capabilities. OpenAI says the suit singles it out over an industry-wide problem. The case stems from the July 2026 incident in which experimental OpenAI agents accessed the internet and breached the internal systems of the AI platform Hugging Face, the BBC reported. According to NPR, the complaint says OpenAI admitted to the attorney general’s office that it “lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing” — more than it has disclosed publicly — and accuses the company of poor security practices, stonewalling the state’s investigation and discouraging employees from raising safety concerns. The state alleges public nuisance and violations of its unfair-competition law. An OpenAI spokesperson said the company has engaged constructively with the attorney general’s office and will continue to do so.
stories.why: This is one of the first attempts by a U.S. state to hold an AI developer legally responsible for what its autonomous agents do online. Because California is home to most leading AI labs, the case could set the bar for how they test and disclose agents that can act on the internet.

stories.headline: Raye leads the Grammy nominations with 11, as Beyoncé earns her 100th nod and BTS sit out the new Asian pop category
stories.deck: British singer Raye led Monday’s Grammy nominations with 11, including album of the year, followed by Rosalía with nine. Beyoncé received her 100th career nomination.
stories.summary: British singer Raye led Monday’s Grammy nominations with 11, including album of the year, followed by Rosalía with nine. Beyoncé received her 100th career nomination. Raye’s nods include record and song of the year for “Where Is My Husband!” and album of the year for This Music May Contain Hope; DW said her total ties the record for a female artist in a single year that Beyoncé set at the 2025 Grammys. Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers, Miranda Lambert and first-time nominee Ella Langley have seven each, and Taylor Swift five. The album of the year field also includes Bridgers, Olivia Dean, Langley, Bruno Mars — the only man in the category — Rodrigo, Swift and Rosalía. In the new best Asian pop music performance category, Bini, Ive and Lisa are nominated; BTS did not submit music, saying they did not want it “divided by region or language.” Dolly Parton, who died in August, received three posthumous nominations. Final voting runs Dec. 10 to Jan. 7, and the ceremony is scheduled for Feb. 7 in Los Angeles.
stories.why: A field led by women — and the BTS boycott of the Asian pop award — will frame the next three months of debate over who the Recording Academy rewards and how it slices global pop into categories. The academy’s chief also used the announcement to stress honouring “human creators” as AI music spreads.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Freeman Johnson, the oldest remaining Pearl Harbor survivor, dies at 106
stories.deck: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining survivors of the Dec. 7, 1941, attack on Pearl Harbor, died on Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts, his daughter told the Associated Press. He was 106.
stories.summary: Freeman Johnson, the oldest of the few remaining survivors of the Dec. 7, 1941, attack on Pearl Harbor, died on Saturday at his home in Centerville, Massachusetts, his daughter told the Associated Press. He was 106. Johnson was working below deck on a boiler of the light cruiser USS St. Louis during the Japanese attack and told the AP in May that he neither saw nor heard it — “I was inside a steam drum.” He later helped commission the battleship USS Iowa and watched Japan’s surrender in Tokyo Bay from the Iowa’s mast in September 1945. After the war he worked in a machinist shop, a convenience store and delivering meals to seniors, retiring from that last job at 90. The list of known survivors had stood at about a dozen names after the death of Ira “Ike” Schab, 105, in December 2025.
stories.why: With the 85th anniversary of Pearl Harbor three weeks away, only a handful of people who were there are still alive. Johnson’s matter-of-fact memories — of missing the attack entirely below deck — are a reminder of how ordinary most of the sailors were.

stories.headline: Carney and Xi agree to lift Chinese tariffs on Canadian pork and seafood in return for more steel and aluminum relief
stories.deck: Meeting in Shenzhen on Tuesday ahead of APEC, Mark Carney and Xi Jinping agreed that China will drop a 25 per cent tariff on frozen pork cuts and several seafood products, worth about $400 million in Canadian exports a year, Carney’s office said.
stories.summary: Meeting in Shenzhen on Tuesday ahead of APEC, Mark Carney and Xi Jinping agreed that China will drop a 25 per cent tariff on frozen pork cuts and several seafood products, worth about $400 million in Canadian exports a year, Carney’s office said. The list includes frozen cold-water shrimp, Greenland halibut, some mollusks and sea cucumber, Global News reported. In return, Canada will extend tariff relief to 32 more Chinese steel and aluminum items for which Canadian supply is short, and its existing remission measures will run two more years. China also agreed to open its market to Canadian fava beans, chickpeas and lentils; the two sides plan a major Canadian trade mission in 2027 and have named next year a “year of e-commerce.” Carney hailed “greater predictability and stability” and said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of raising exports to China “by 50% by the end of this decade,” DW reported. Xi, according to Xinhua as carried by RTHK, set out four proposals for relations and said exchanges had fully resumed. Before the trip, Carney said he would raise foreign interference, which Beijing denies. On Monday, U.S. trade adviser Peter Navarro called Carney’s suggestion that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if talks with Washington fail “offensive in the extreme.”
stories.why: Ottawa is using China to cut its dependence on the U.S. market while trade talks with Washington drag on. That brings quick wins for farmers and fishers, but it also feeds the White House’s anger and Canadian worries about security and election interference.

stories.headline: Quebecor makes a $31-billion bid for Telus, whose board says the offer carries significant risks
stories.deck: Quebecor, owner of Videotron, Freedom Mobile and Fizz, has proposed to buy Telus in a cash-and-shares deal it values at about $31 billion, a premium of roughly 60 per cent. Telus’s board says it is reviewing the offer but has serious concerns.
stories.summary: Quebecor, owner of Videotron, Freedom Mobile and Fizz, has proposed to buy Telus in a cash-and-shares deal it values at about $31 billion, a premium of roughly 60 per cent. Telus’s board says it is reviewing the offer but has serious concerns. Under the non-binding proposal, Telus shareholders would get $6.35 in cash and 0.17 of a Quebecor share for each Telus share. Quebecor said it first approached Telus in June and sent an enhanced offer this month; it says it would keep the Telus brands and that a combined company could invest more in 5G and rural connectivity. Telus board chair John Manley said Quebecor had yet to explain how the deal could win approval under Canada’s telecom rules and disputed its valuation, and that Telus would keep engaging with Quebecor, the government and regulators while exploring alternatives. Any deal would need approval from the Competition Bureau, the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada; Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said it would be reviewed “independently and rigorously.”
stories.why: Quebecor became Canada’s low-price challenger by buying Freedom Mobile; taking over Telus would turn it into one of the giants and cut the number of national carriers. Experts cited by CBC say the deal would make the market less competitive and could affect phone bills, so regulators’ verdict matters to customers, not just shareholders.

stories.headline: P.E.I. fisherman and carpenter Nicholas Herring wins the $100,000 Giller Prize for Your Breath in Charcoal
stories.deck: Nicholas Herring of Murray Harbour, P.E.I., won the 2026 Giller Prize on Monday night in Toronto for Your Breath in Charcoal, his second novel. For the first time, the winner was chosen by a jury of independent booksellers.
stories.summary: Nicholas Herring of Murray Harbour, P.E.I., won the 2026 Giller Prize on Monday night in Toronto for Your Breath in Charcoal, his second novel. For the first time, the winner was chosen by a jury of independent booksellers. The novel follows Knickle, an East Coast “everyman” on a road trip from P.E.I. to Toronto; CBC describes it as the story of two Islanders in the late 1990s trying to make it in Ontario’s construction industry. The nine-member jury called it “an uproarious, undeniably Maritime tale.” Published by Goose Lane Editions, it beat finalists Tara Gereaux, Michelle Good, Nazanine Hozar and Patmeena Sabit, who each receive $10,000. Herring, who works as a fisherman and carpenter, won the Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize for his debut, Some Hellish. CBC reported that he said he wrote the book to change the lives of his wife and daughter: “I guess it changed my life, too.”
stories.why: The Giller is Canada’s richest fiction prize and reliably lifts sales, so a small Atlantic press and a writer who still fishes for a living are about to get national attention. A booksellers’ jury picking a funny, working-class road novel also suggests the prize is reaching for everyday readers.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported

stories.headline: Meta tells senators it would have to consider pulling encrypted services from Canada if the lawful-access bill passes unchanged
stories.deck: Meta representatives told a Senate committee on Monday evening that Bill C-22 could leave the company unable to offer secure end-to-end encryption in Canada, and that it would have to “consider” withdrawing such services if the bill passes as is.
stories.summary: Meta representatives told a Senate committee on Monday evening that Bill C-22 could leave the company unable to offer secure end-to-end encryption in Canada, and that it would have to “consider” withdrawing such services if the bill passes as is. The lawful-access bill would require tech companies to be able to hand over information to investigators with a warrant and would let the public safety minister issue confidential orders requiring them to build in surveillance capabilities, subject to review by the intelligence commissioner. Meta’s privacy policy director, Robyn Greene, said the law would be impossible to comply with “and still offer secure, end-to-end encrypted services.” Signal told the committee it would leave Canada rather than compromise users’ security, and Apple has said the government’s amendments are not enough. The government argues police need the tools to fight modern crime; it has already narrowed when companies must decrypt data and cut metadata retention to six months.
stories.why: WhatsApp, Signal and iMessage are how millions of Canadians talk, so a standoff over encryption could change everyday communication. The Senate committee’s next moves will show whether Ottawa adds stronger protections or tests the companies’ threats.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported

stories.headline: Mark Scheifele passes Dale Hawerchuk as the Jets’ all-time points leader and is named the NHL’s first star of the week
stories.deck: Winnipeg Jets forward Mark Scheifele was named the NHL’s first star of the week on Monday after eight points in three games, a week in which he passed Dale Hawerchuk atop the franchise’s all-time points list.
stories.summary: Winnipeg Jets forward Mark Scheifele was named the NHL’s first star of the week on Monday after eight points in three games, a week in which he passed Dale Hawerchuk atop the franchise’s all-time points list. He also overtook Thomas Steen for the Jets’ assists record and tied Hawerchuk’s franchise goals mark of 379, Global News reported. The run helped Winnipeg extend its winning streak to six games, capped by a four-point comeback win over the Chicago Blackhawks. After a slow start, the 33-year-old has seven goals and 19 assists in 21 games, tied with Kyle Connor for the team lead. It is the 10th time he has been named a player of the week.
stories.why: Hawerchuk is the Jets’ defining star, so Scheifele overtaking him is a landmark for a club that has spent more than a decade building around him. One more goal gives him the franchise goals record as well.

stories.headline: Hong Kong’s unemployment rate edges down to 3.8%, with the clearest drop in restaurants and bars
stories.deck: Hong Kong’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell to 3.8 per cent in August to October from 3.9 per cent in the previous three months, the government said on Tuesday. Underemployment stayed at 2.0 per cent.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate fell to 3.8 per cent in August to October from 3.9 per cent in the previous three months, the government said on Tuesday. Underemployment stayed at 2.0 per cent. Unemployment fell in many sectors, most noticeably in food and beverage services. The number of unemployed people dropped by about 4,500 to 150,500, but total employment also slipped by about 1,200 to 3,653,800 and the labour force shrank by about 5,800 to 3,804,200. Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun called the market “broadly stable” and said economic growth, consumption and rising tourism should support jobs, while the government watches external uncertainties.
stories.why: The gain in restaurants fits the government’s upbeat growth outlook. But because the workforce shrank, part of the fall reflects fewer people working or looking for work, not only more hiring.

stories.deck: Chief Executive John Lee arrived in Shenzhen on Tuesday for this week’s APEC leaders’ meeting, saying he hoped to promote Hong Kong’s role during China’s year as host.
stories.summary: Chief Executive John Lee arrived in Shenzhen on Tuesday for this week’s APEC leaders’ meeting, saying he hoped to promote Hong Kong’s role during China’s year as host. He was received by a representative of the Communist Party’s Hong Kong and Macao Work Office, RTHK reported. Lee pointed to last month’s APEC finance ministers’ meeting, held in Hong Kong for the first time, as evidence of the city’s role in connecting the mainland and the world. During the trip he is scheduled to attend the APEC CEO Summit and hold bilateral meetings with leaders of other economies. He called Shenzhen and Hong Kong “sister cities” that have advanced side by side in AI and technology.
stories.why: Hong Kong takes part in APEC as a separate economy, one of the few global forums where its leader sits with heads of government. Lee wants the week to show investors that the city still works as China’s bridge to the world while Beijing is centre stage.

stories.headline: A woman’s ovaries were removed by mistake during surgery at CUHK Medical Centre, Hong Kong health officials disclose
stories.deck: Hong Kong’s Department of Health disclosed on Tuesday that both ovaries of a 45-year-old woman were wrongly removed during a hysterectomy at the private CUHK Medical Centre in September. She is in stable condition.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s Department of Health disclosed on Tuesday that both ovaries of a 45-year-old woman were wrongly removed during a hysterectomy at the private CUHK Medical Centre in September. She is in stable condition. The woman had been undergoing a laparoscopic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingectomy, the removal of both fallopian tubes. The department said it found no evidence that the hospital had breached its code of practice on premises, staffing or equipment. The hospital said it was highly concerned, had apologised to the patient and her family and would make improvements after a review. The department also disclosed a second September case in which a 27-year-old woman at a day procedure centre was mistaken for another patient and given dental scaling. Both facilities submitted investigation reports, which the department said it has reviewed.
stories.why: Removing both ovaries at 45 brings on early menopause, so this is a life-changing error. The cases surfaced only when officials answered media questions two months later, which raises questions about how quickly serious incidents at private hospitals are made public.

stories.headline: Privacy watchdog opens a compliance check on a facial-recognition entry system at Lam Tin’s Laguna City estate
stories.deck: Hong Kong’s privacy commissioner has started a compliance check on a plan by Laguna City’s property manager to install facial-recognition access at the Lam Tin estate, which may involve more than 8,000 households, Hong Kong Free Press reported.
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s privacy commissioner has started a compliance check on a plan by Laguna City’s property manager to install facial-recognition access at the Lam Tin estate, which may involve more than 8,000 households, Hong Kong Free Press reported. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data said on Friday that facial images are sensitive personal data and that it had asked the manager, Citybase Property Management, for more information. Citybase said on Monday it would cooperate and handle residents’ biometric data lawfully, and that the system, being installed in three of the estate’s four phases, would make life more convenient. Kwun Tong District Councillor Tang Wing-chun said on an RTHK programme that he had heard from residents both for and against the plan, and that the system was set to go live in January.
stories.why: Facial recognition is spreading in Hong Kong — police have activated it across their AI-enabled CCTV network — and this is an early test of how the privacy law applies where people live. The outcome could guide other estates weighing similar systems.

stories.headline: Beijing says Thursday’s Xi–Trump–Putin talks will cover “world peace”; Trump lists nuclear arms, Iran and Ukraine
stories.deck: China said the first three-way summit of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, due in Shenzhen on Thursday, will hold “in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.”
stories.summary: China said the first three-way summit of Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, due in Shenzhen on Thursday, will hold “in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.” Foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Monday it would be of “ground-breaking significance,” AFP reported via Hong Kong Free Press. Leaving the White House on Monday, Trump said the leaders would discuss the “tough subject” of denuclearisation, Iran, trade and “my favourite subject, Ukraine,” and that North Korea’s Kim Jong Un “may come” to China, which was “up to President Xi.” Beijing has long said the U.S. and Russia should cut their arsenals before China joins arms talks. Separately, the chair of APEC’s senior officials said consultations on the leaders’ outcome document for the APEC meeting had begun, RTHK reported.
stories.why: Beijing’s wording keeps expectations vague while Trump promises a broad agenda, so the gap between them is the thing to watch. Ukraine fears a deal over its head, and any sign of China joining nuclear talks would be a genuine first.

stories.summary: Xi Jinping met Vietnam’s leader To Lam in Shenzhen on Tuesday morning, before the APEC summit, and said the more turbulent the world becomes, the more China and Vietnam must “stand together as comrades and brothers,” China’s foreign ministry said. Xi called for faster work on smart ports, cross-border economic zones, digital and green cooperation and AI, and said the two should “properly manage maritime differences” — disputes that centre on the South China Sea. stories.headline: China charges Gu Jun, former head of state nuclear giant CNNC, with taking bribes
stories.deck: Prosecutors have charged Gu Jun, the former general manager of China National Nuclear Corporation, with accepting bribes of an “especially huge” amount, China’s Supreme People’s Procuratorate said on Tuesday, according to state media.
stories.summary: Prosecutors have charged Gu Jun, the former general manager of China National Nuclear Corporation, with accepting bribes of an “especially huge” amount, China’s Supreme People’s Procuratorate said on Tuesday, according to state media. The indictment, filed with a court in Enshi, Hubei province, accuses Gu of using his posts to secure benefits for others in exchange for money and valuables, China Daily reported. Gu, 63, spent four decades in the nuclear industry — he was among the first reactor operators involved in building the Qinshan plant, China’s first domestically designed nuclear power station — and ran CNNC from 2018 until he retired in 2024. He was placed under investigation in January and expelled from the Communist Party in July. The charges have not been tested in court.
stories.why: CNNC builds China’s reactors and runs its nuclear fuel cycle, and Gu is among the most senior nuclear-industry figures caught in Xi Jinping’s anti-graft drive, which has swept through defence and strategic industries.

stories.headline: Shanghai fires two scientists after a probe into a child’s death following an experimental gene-editing treatment
stories.deck: Shanghai authorities have dismissed two researchers after investigators found ignored safety warnings, weak ethics review and undisclosed money and gifts from the family in a gene-editing trial that ended in a child’s death, Sixth Tone reported.
stories.summary: Shanghai authorities have dismissed two researchers after investigators found ignored safety warnings, weak ethics review and undisclosed money and gifts from the family in a gene-editing trial that ended in a child’s death, Sixth Tone reported. The child, who had a rare neurodevelopmental disorder, died seven days after an injection at Xinhua Hospital in March 2025. The family had contributed 5.3 million yuan (about US$800,000) to the research and separately gave researchers about 1.06 million yuan in money and gifts, investigators said. The team’s February 2026 paper in Nature did not mention the death. Investigators found no data fabrication in the paper but said the team failed to share a safety report from monkey experiments with the trial’s lead investigator. Qiu Zilong and Yang Kan were dismissed and barred from science programmes for five years; hospital officials were demoted, and the city plans special inspections of clinical research on new biomedical technologies.
stories.why: China is racing to lead in gene and cell therapies, and this case shows how experimental treatment can outrun safeguards. Stricter oversight of such trials is likely to follow.

stories.headline: China adds a CAR T-cell cancer therapy to its national health insurance for the first time, from Jan. 1
stories.deck: China will cover a CAR T-cell therapy under its national basic medical insurance for the first time from Jan. 1, making a lymphoma treatment that costs 1.29 million yuan a dose far more affordable, Sixth Tone reported.
stories.summary: China will cover a CAR T-cell therapy under its national basic medical insurance for the first time from Jan. 1, making a lymphoma treatment that costs 1.29 million yuan a dose far more affordable, Sixth Tone reported. The National Healthcare Security Administration said on Nov. 14 that relmacabtagene autoleucel (relma-cel), sold by Shanghai-based JW Therapeutics as Carteyva, will be added to the reimbursement list, which gains 107 drugs for cancer, chronic, mental, rare and childhood illnesses. CAR T therapy re-engineers a patient’s own immune cells to attack cancer. Such drugs had long been left off the list because of their price, and their use in China lags far behind the U.S. and Europe. About 1.33 billion people were enrolled in basic medical insurance at the end of 2025.
stories.why: Million-yuan cell therapies have been out of reach for most Chinese patients; adding one to basic insurance signals Beijing will pay for some cutting-edge treatment. How much patients still pay out of pocket will decide how many can use it.

stories.headline: Five EU countries plan a “return hub” in Rwanda for rejected asylum seekers, with first transfers targeted by the end of 2027
stories.deck: Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Greece announced on Monday that they are working with Rwanda on a “return hub” for migrants who have no legal right to stay in the European Union. A formal agreement has not yet been signed.
stories.summary: Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Greece announced on Monday that they are working with Rwanda on a “return hub” for migrants who have no legal right to stay in the European Union. A formal agreement has not yet been signed. Unlike Britain’s abandoned Rwanda plan, which would have sent people there while their claims were processed, the scheme would cover only people whose asylum applications have already been rejected and who cannot be returned home. They could settle in Rwanda, go home or move to another country that admits them. The governments, which would pay the costs, did not say how many people would be sent. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the plan would “break down the business model of human smugglers.” Rwanda’s interior minister said Kigali was not planning for thousands to stay. Human Rights Watch called the plan “utterly deplorable,” and 47 organisations urged the countries to scrap it.
stories.why: The five governments call it a pilot and a deterrent, so if it goes ahead other European states may copy it. Critics point out that Europe has repeatedly raised concerns about Rwanda’s human rights record and its support for the M23 armed group in eastern Congo.
stories.label: Official statement + Reported

stories.headline: Mongolia’s president says he will resign over railway bribery allegations he calls false
stories.deck: Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa said on Tuesday he would step down after the opposition accused him of taking money linked to a coal railway to the Chinese border. He says he is being defamed and will cooperate with investigators.
stories.summary: Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa said on Tuesday he would step down after the opposition accused him of taking money linked to a coal railway to the Chinese border. He says he is being defamed and will cooperate with investigators. A former mayor of Ulaanbaatar from a rival faction of the president’s own party alleged on Saturday that Khurelsukh received $25 million connected to the Tavantolgoi–Gashuunsukhait railway, which carries coal to China, DW reported; the opposition Democratic Party then called for him to quit. The company that built the line, Bodi International, has denied paying bribes. Khurelsukh said he would hand over his duties so “the truth can be established,” CNA reported, citing the state news agency Montsame. His resignation takes effect only if parliament, the State Great Khural, accepts it.
stories.why: Mongolia is a democracy squeezed between Russia and China, and coal exports to China fund much of its budget. A president quitting over a coal-railway contract deepens political turmoil after three prime ministers in nine months.

stories.headline: COP31 draft text calls for an “immediate transition away from fossil fuels” as the Antalya climate talks enter their final week
stories.deck: A draft political deal tabled by COP31 co-host Australia calls for an “immediate transition away from fossil fuels” and for adaptation finance for developing countries to triple to at least $120 billion. Negotiators aim to agree a final text by Friday.
stories.summary: A draft political deal tabled by COP31 co-host Australia calls for an “immediate transition away from fossil fuels” and for adaptation finance for developing countries to triple to at least $120 billion. Negotiators aim to agree a final text by Friday. The 18-page draft, released on Monday in Antalya, Türkiye, also includes co-host Türkiye’s goal of raising electrification of the world economy to 35 per cent by 2035, expresses “deep concern” that the 1.5C warming limit is now out of reach, and calls for rapidly scaling up carbon capture and removal. Greenpeace Germany said it held “all the necessary building blocks,” while others warned it lacked binding commitments or read “like a Christmas wish list.” Australia’s climate minister, Chris Bowen, called the talks “very constructive.”
stories.why: Oil producers have fought this kind of wording at every COP, so whether “immediate transition” survives to Friday is the real test. The draft’s admission that 1.5C is slipping away also shifts the talks toward overshoot and adaptation money.

stories.headline: Robert Pattinson is named the seventh James Bond, with Denis Villeneuve set to direct the next 007 film
stories.deck: Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson will succeed Daniel Craig as James Bond, making the 40-year-old British actor the seventh to play the role in the official films.
stories.summary: Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson will succeed Daniel Craig as James Bond, making the 40-year-old British actor the seventh to play the role in the official films. The franchise’s social media accounts were wiped and replaced with the message “Identity confirmed” before a first photo of Pattinson in a tuxedo was released, the Guardian reported. Pattinson called the role “the honour of a lifetime.” The 26th Bond film, as yet untitled, will be directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight, and is due for release in 2028, the BBC said. It will be the first made since longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson handed creative control to Amazon MGM in 2025. Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner were among those reported to have been in contention. Buckingham Palace welcomed him on Instagram: “Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond.”
stories.why: Bond is one of cinema’s most valuable franchises, and this is Amazon’s first big creative decision since taking it over. Picking a bankable star known for arthouse choices signals it wants both blockbuster box office and critical credibility.
